nodes.notes: Remote method signatures follow the module spec and README (websocket 2.16.x).

nodes.title: ballerina/websub
nodes.summary: The WebSub library implements the W3C WebSub subscriber role as a `websub:Listener` service that subscribes to a hub topic, verifies intent and receives content distribution (webhook) notifications.

must_cover.text: Write a subscriber with `@websub:SubscriberServiceConfig {target: ["<HUB_URL>", "<TOPIC_URL>"], leaseSeconds: 36000}` on `service /subscriber on new websub:Listener(9090)`, implementing `remote function onEventNotification(websub:ContentDistributionMessage event)` that returns `websub:ACKNOWLEDGEMENT`

Implement the optional callbacks `onSubscriptionVerification` (returning `websub:SUBSCRIPTION_VERIFICATION_SUCCESS` or an error), `onUnsubscriptionVerification` (`websub:UNSUBSCRIPTION_VERIFICATION_SUCCESS`) and `onSubscriptionValidationDenied(websub:SubscriptionDeniedError)`
Let the subscriber discover the hub and topic by giving a single resource URL as `target: "RESOURCE_URL"` in `@websub:SubscriberServiceConfig`
Omit the service path to let the listener generate one, and set a public `callback` URL (e.g. an ngrok URL) with `appendServicePath: true` when the subscriber runs behind a tunnel

Use a WebSub subscriber as a webhook receiver (e.g. for GitHub) by setting `secret` for authenticated content distribution and `httpConfig: {auth: {token: ...}}`, and read the payload from `event.content` with `ensureType()` into `json` or a record
Unsubscribe automatically on shutdown with `unsubscribeOnShutdown: true` together with `websub:ListenerConfiguration {gracefulShutdownPeriod: 15}`

Return `error` from subscriber remote methods and know how each is interpreted (verification failure for the verification callbacks, still acknowledged for `onEventNotification`), and return `websub:SubscriptionDeletedError` from `onEventNotification` when the subscriber no longer needs updates (sent as 410 Gone)

out_of_scope: Implementing a hub or publishing updates (lib.websubhub)
HTTP client configuration details (lib.http)

edges.note: Subscriber side vs hub/publisher side of WebSub

nodes.notes: Items come from the module README and the single WebSub BBE (websub 2.x).

nodes.title: ballerina/websubhub
nodes.summary: The WebSubHub library implements the WebSub hub role as a `websubhub:Service` on a `websubhub:Listener`, plus a `websubhub:HubClient` for delivering content to subscribers and a `websubhub:PublisherClient` for registering topics and publishing updates.

must_cover.text: Create a `websubhub:Listener` from a port or an `http:Listener` and attach a hub service declaratively (`service /hub on new websubhub:Listener(9090)`) or programmatically with `attach`, `'start` and `gracefulStop`

Implement `remote function onRegisterTopic(websubhub:TopicRegistration msg)` and `onDeregisterTopic(websubhub:TopicDeregistration msg)` returning `websubhub:TOPIC_REGISTRATION_SUCCESS`/`websubhub:TOPIC_REGISTRATION_ERROR` and the deregistration counterparts
Accept publisher content updates in `remote function onUpdateMessage(websubhub:UpdateMessage msg)` returning `websubhub:ACKNOWLEDGEMENT` or `websubhub:UPDATE_MESSAGE_ERROR`

Handle subscriptions with `onSubscription(websubhub:Subscription msg)` (returning `websubhub:SUBSCRIPTION_ACCEPTED` or `websubhub:BAD_SUBSCRIPTION_ERROR`), `onSubscriptionValidation` (returning `websubhub:SUBSCRIPTION_DENIED_ERROR` to reject) and `onSubscriptionIntentVerified(websubhub:VerifiedSubscription msg)`, plus the matching `onUnsubscription*` methods

Configure the hub with `@websubhub:ServiceConfig {leaseSeconds, webHookConfig, autoVerifySubscriptionIntent}` and, with auto-verification on, take a `websubhub:Controller` parameter in `onSubscription` to call `markAsVerified()`
Deliver content to a verified subscriber by creating `websubhub:HubClient` from the subscription message (`check new (msg)`) and calling `notifyContentDistribution({content: ...})`
Act as a publisher with `websubhub:PublisherClient` created from the hub URL, calling `registerTopic(topic)`, `deregisterTopic(topic)`, `publishUpdate(topic, payload)` and `notifyUpdate(topic)`

Return `error` from hub remote methods and know the meaning for each (e.g. topic registration failure for `onRegisterTopic`, internal server error for `onSubscription`, validation failure for `onSubscriptionValidation`)

out_of_scope: The subscriber side of WebSub (lib.websub)
Underlying HTTP client settings reused by `websubhub:ClientConfiguration` (lib.http)
nodes.notes: The README's HubClient sample types `onSubscriptionIntentVerified` with `websubhub:Subscription`, while the spec's service type uses `websubhub:VerifiedSubscription`; items follow the spec. Spec section 2.2.2.3 is headed `onEventMessage` but the service type and README use `onUpdateMessage`.

nodes.title: ballerina/xslt
nodes.summary: The `xslt` module transforms single-rooted XML into another XML, HTML or plain-text form using an XSLT 1.0 stylesheet through the `xslt:transform` function.

must_cover.text: Transform an XML value with an XSL stylesheet held as an `xml` value using `xml target = check xslt:transform(sourceXml, xsl);`
Write an XSLT 1.0 stylesheet (`xsl:stylesheet version="1.0"` with `xsl:template`, `xsl:for-each` and `xsl:value-of`) that renders XML records as an HTML table, and embed it as an XML template literal
Use `xslt:transform` to restructure XML into a different XML schema or to produce plain text, knowing that only XSLT version 1.0 is supported
Load the source XML and the stylesheet from files with `io:fileReadXml` before calling `xslt:transform`, and write the result with `io:fileWriteXml`
Pass parameters into the stylesheet with the third argument `params`, a `map<string|decimal|xml>` such as `{"currency": "USD"}`, read in the stylesheet through `xsl:param`
Provide a single-rooted XML element as the input, since `xslt:transform` transforms single-rooted XML content
Handle the `error` returned when the input or stylesheet cannot be transformed (the module defines `xslt:TransformError`), using `check` or an `is error` test

out_of_scope: XML literals, navigation and mutation in the language (concept.xml, lib.lang.xml)
XML to record conversion and XPath queries (lib.data.xmldata)

sources.note: transform(xml input, xml xsl, map<string|decimal|xml> params = {}) returns xml|error

nodes.notes: Verified against module-ballerina-xslt master 2.9.3 (= latest tag). The params argument is documented only as 'Optional parameters passed into the xslt template'; the `xsl:param` binding is standard XSLT behaviour, not shown in a Ballerina example.

nodes.title: bal
nodes.summary: `bal` is the Ballerina build tool and package manager. It builds, runs, formats and documents packages and single files, and manages installed Ballerina distributions.

must_cover.text: Discover commands with `bal help`, `bal help <command>` (e.g. `bal help pull`) and `bal <command> --help`, and print the distribution, language specification and update tool versions with `bal version`

Run a program with `bal run` for the current package, `bal run app.bal` for a single file or `bal run target/bin/app.jar` for a built JAR, and pass program arguments to `main` after `--`, e.g. `bal run -- add 10 5`
Give values to configurable variables when running, e.g. `bal run -- -Cval1=add -Cval2=10`, alongside or instead of a `Config.toml` file

Build an executable JAR with `bal build` (written to `target/bin/`) or `bal build app.bal` for a single file (written to the current directory, renamed with `-o <output>`), knowing individual `.bal` files of a package cannot be built on their own
Use common build flags: `--offline`, `--sticky`, `--target-dir <path>`, `--observability-included`, `--experimental` for experimental language features, and `--show-dependency-diagnostics`

Produce other build outputs: container and Kubernetes artifacts with `bal build --cloud=docker` or `--cloud=k8s`, a native image with `--graalvm` and `--graalvm-build-options="..."`, and OpenAPI definitions for services with `--export-openapi`
Re-run a service project automatically on file changes with `bal run --watch` (experimental), and start a program for remote debugging with `bal run --debug <port>`
Delete build outputs with `bal clean`, or a custom output directory with `bal clean --target-dir <path>`
Format code to the coding conventions with `bal format` for the package, `bal format <module>` or `bal format app.bal`, and preview the files that would change with `bal format -d`/`--dry-run`

Customize formatting with a `Format.toml` file (or `[format]` `configPath` in `Ballerina.toml`) using sections such as `[indent]` `indentSize`, `[wrapping]` `maxLineLength`, `[braces]` `functionBraceStyle = "NewLine"`, `[functionDefinition]` `parametersWrap = "ChopDown"`, `[import]` `sortImports` and `[query]` `alignMultiLineQueries`

Write documentation comments (`#` lines with `+ param - description` and `+ return - description`) and generate HTML API docs with `bal doc` into `target/apidocs`, using `-o <dir>` for another output directory and `-e` to exclude modules

Manage installed distributions with `bal dist list`, `bal dist update`, `bal dist pull <version>`, `bal dist use <version>` and `bal dist remove <version>`, and update the `bal` tool itself with `bal update`
Try snippets in the experimental REPL with `bal shell`, using `/imports`, `/vars`, `/dclns`, `/file <FILE>`, `/remove <NAMES>`, `/reset` and `/exit`
Profile a package or file with the experimental `bal profile` command, which runs the program and writes a flame graph to `ProfilerReport.html` in the target directory

out_of_scope: `bal new`, `bal add` and package layout (tool.packages)
`bal test` and its options (tool.bal_test)
`bal pack`, `bal push`, `bal pull`, `bal search`, `bal semver`, `bal deprecate` (tool.central)
Dependency locking with `--sticky`/`--offline` and `bal graph` (tool.dependencies_toml)
Installing tools with `bal tool` (tool.bal_tool)
Code generators such as `bal openapi`, `bal grpc`, `bal persist` (tool.bal_openapi, tool.bal_grpc, tool.bal_persist)
Docker, Kubernetes and GraalVM build details (tool.code_to_cloud, tool.graalvm)

sources.note: bal command help texts (build, run, clean, format, doc, profile)

nodes.notes: The docs show running a built JAR with `bal run target/bin/<name>.jar`. Commands such as `dist` and `version` are handled by the tool itself; `build`, `run`, `test`, `pull` and `push` are delegated to the active distribution.

nodes.title: bal asyncapi
nodes.summary: The `bal asyncapi` CLI tool generates a Ballerina listener, service types and an event dispatcher from an AsyncAPI 2.x contract for an HTTP-based event API (webhooks), so you can implement one remote method per event type.

must_cover.text: Add `x-ballerina-event-identifier` with `type` and `path` at the top of the contract so the listener can find the event type in an incoming request (only `type: "body"`, with `path` as the JSON path such as `event.type`, is currently supported)
Mark every message in a channel (e.g. each entry under `subscribe: message: oneOf:`) with `x-ballerina-event-type` set to that event's name, such as `"app_mention"`

Generate sources with `bal asyncapi -i <contract> [-o <dir>]`, which writes `data_types.bal` (types from the contract), `service_types.bal` (the service types for the event API), `listener.bal` (the HTTP listener) and the dispatcher service file with the event-dispatching logic

Run the generated code as a package (`bal init` in the output directory) and implement a service on the generated listener with one remote method per event, e.g. `listener Listener webhookListener = new (8090);` and `service AppService on webhookListener { remote function onAppMention(GenericEventWrapper event) returns error? { ... } }`
Add logic such as authentication of incoming calls to the resource method of the generated dispatcher service, which receives every incoming request
Extend the `init` function in the generated `listener.bal` when the listener needs secrets, endpoint URLs or tokens

out_of_scope: Writing HTTP listeners and services by hand (lib.http)
Event-driven design in general (topic.event_driven)
nodes.notes: Docs: AsyncAPI 2.x only and HTTP-based event APIs only; the tool can be updated with `bal tool update asyncapi`. The docs spell the dispatcher file as both `dispacther_service.bal` and `dispatcher_service.bal`, so items do not name it. The asyncapi-tools README mentions client generation for `ws` and exporting AsyncAPI from services, but no command syntax is documented, so those are left out. Example generated modules: ballerinax/trigger.slack, ballerinax/trigger.twilio.

nodes.title: bal bindgen
nodes.summary: The `bal bindgen` CLI tool generates Ballerina binding classes and functions for Java classes, built on `ballerina/jballerina.java` interop, so a Ballerina program can call Java libraries without writing the FFI layer by hand.

must_cover.text: Generate bindings with `bal bindgen [-cp <jar-or-dir>,...] <fully.qualified.ClassName>...`, listing the class names last; no classpath is needed for standard Java libraries, libraries in the Ballerina SDK or platform libraries already declared in `Ballerina.toml`

Use `-mvn <groupId>:<artifactId>:<version>` (e.g. `bal bindgen -mvn org.yaml:snakeyaml:1.25 org.yaml.snakeyaml.Yaml java.io.FileInputStream`) to resolve a library and its transitive dependencies into `target/platform-libs` and add them to `Ballerina.toml` as platform libraries

Import the generated modules (one per Java package by default, e.g. `import yaml_package.java.io as javaio;`), or put all bindings in one directory with `-o <path>` and make them public with `--public`

Recognise a generated binding class: a `distinct class` with the Java simple name, annotated `@java:Binding {'class: "java.util.ArrayDeque"}`, including `*java:JObject`, holding the Java object in `public handle jObj` and set up by `function init(handle obj)`
Create Java objects through the generated constructor functions outside the class, named `new<ClassName>` with a number per overload (e.g. `newArrayDeque1()`, `newArrayDeque2(int arg0)`)

Call Java instance methods as methods of the binding class (overloads get a numeric suffix) and static methods as module functions prefixed with the class name (e.g. `UUID_randomUUID()` for `UUID.randomUUID()`)

Read and write public Java fields through generated getters and setters: `get<FIELD>()` and `set<FIELD>(value)` methods for instance fields, and `<Class>_get<FIELD>()` and `<Class>_set<FIELD>(value)` functions for static fields (no setter for final fields)

Handle Java exceptions as the generated Ballerina error types of the same name (e.g. `read()` returns `int|IOException`), narrowing with a type test such as `if fileInputStream is javaio:FileNotFoundException`; an exception class generated explicitly as a binding class is named with a `J` prefix (e.g. `JFileNotFoundException`)

Know that Java classes used in the generated APIs get empty binding classes (only `jObj`, `init` and `toString`) that you fill in by running the tool again for them, that `java.lang.String` maps to `string`, and that generic methods return `java.lang.Object` bindings because generics are not supported

Apply the Java-to-Ballerina type mapping in generated signatures: `boolean` to `boolean`, `byte` to `byte`, `int`/`short`/`char`/`long` to `int`, `float`/`double` to `float`, `String` to `string`, and other classes to binding classes

Pass Java `null` through bindings by generating nilable parameter and return types with `--with-optional-types`, or only for parameters with `--with-optional-types-param` or only for returns with `--with-optional-types-return`

Assign a binding of a Java subclass to its superclass binding (e.g. `InputStream inputStream = check newFileInputStream3("sample.txt");`), which works through type inclusion, and cast back down with `FileInputStream f = check java:cast(inputStream);`
Generate bindings for inner classes with the `Outer$Inner` form, escaping the dollar sign in the shell (e.g. `bal bindgen java.lang.Character\$Subset`)
Use generated bindings in a program, e.g. `snakeyaml:Yaml yaml = snakeyaml:newYaml1();` and `javalang:Object mapObj = yaml.load(fileInputStream);`, then `bal build` and `bal run` the package

out_of_scope: Writing interop bindings by hand with `@java:Method` and friends (lib.jballerina.java)
Declaring platform dependencies in Ballerina.toml (tool.ballerina_toml)

sources.note: Call Java code from Ballerina (SnakeYAML walkthrough)

nodes.notes: The docs table marks `--public` as 'Mandatory', but its description says it only applies when bindings go into a single directory, so it is treated as optional here. The docs say generated function names will improve in a future release.

nodes.title: bal edi
nodes.summary: The `bal edi` CLI tool converts EDIFACT, X12 and ESL schemas to the Ballerina EDI schema format and generates records, `fromEdiString`/`toEdiString` parser functions and whole EDI packages (with a REST connector) that run on `ballerina/edi`.

must_cover.text: Install the tool from Ballerina Central with `bal tool pull edi`

Read UN/EDIFACT D03A messages without the tool through the prebuilt `ballerinax/edifact.d03a.*` packages, e.g. `import ballerinax/edifact.d03a.supplychain.mORDERS;` and `mORDERS:interchangeFromEdiString(ediText)`, and generate your own module only for partner variants, X12, other EDIFACT versions or proprietary formats
Convert an EDIFACT specification with `bal edi convertEdifactSchema -v d03a -t ORDERS -i d03a.zip -o resources`, which writes `resources/ORDERS.json` (omit `-t` to convert every message type)

Convert a licensed X12 schema with `bal edi convertX12Schema -i input/850.xsd -o resources/850-schema.json`, adding `-H` for headers (envelope) mode, `-c` for a collection of schemas, or `-d <file>` for separate segment details
Convert an ESL schema with `bal edi convertESL -b segment_definitions.yaml -i esl_schema.esl -o resources/schema.json`

Write a Ballerina EDI schema by hand for a proprietary format: a JSON object with `name`, `delimiters` (`segment`, `field`, `component`, `repetition`) and `segments`, each with `code`, `tag`, `minOccurances`/`maxOccurances` (`-1` for unbounded) and `fields` (`tag`, optional `dataType` such as `int`)

Adapt a converted schema to a trading partner by editing delimiters, occurrence counts, field data types, `ignoreSegments` or the `fields` list of a segment, keep the schema under version control and regenerate after each edit

Generate records and parser functions with `bal edi codegen -i resources/schema.json -o orders.bal` inside a package, giving record types such as `SimpleOrder` and `Header_Type`; generate each schema into its own module in larger projects
Parse EDI text into the generated record with `SimpleOrder order = check fromEdiString(ediText);` and read its fields like any record
Serialize a generated record back to EDI text with `string ediText = check toEdiString(order);`

Work with envelope-aware schemas through the generated `<Name>Interchange`, `<Name>FunctionalGroup` (X12) and `<Name>Transaction` records and the `headersFromEdiString`, `interchangeFromEdiString` and `interchangeToEdiString` functions, checking each transaction's `body` (typed `<Name>|error`) so one bad transaction does not fail the whole parse; this needs `ballerina/edi` 1.6.0 or later

Generate a package for a set of schemas with `bal edi libgen -p citymart/porder -i CityMart/schemas -o CityMart/lib`, which puts each schema in its own module (e.g. `m850`), then `bal pack` and `bal push` it and import modules such as `citymart/porder.m850`

Dispatch by EDI name through the generated package's default module, e.g. `porder:fromEdiString(text, porder:EDI_850)`, `porder:headersFromEdiString(...)` (returns `anydata`) and `porder:interchangeFromEdiString(...)` (returns `any`), narrowing results with `ensureType()`

Build and run a generated EDI package as a REST service with `bal build` and `bal run`, which exposes an EDI-to-JSON endpoint under `edis` (e.g. `/porderParser/edis/850`) and a JSON-to-EDI endpoint under `objects` for each schema

out_of_scope: The `ballerina/edi` library API and schema semantics (lib.edi)

nodes.title: bal graphql
nodes.summary: The `bal graphql` CLI tool exports the GraphQL schema (SDL) of a Ballerina GraphQL service, generates a Ballerina GraphQL service from an SDL schema, and (experimentally) generates Ballerina clients from a `graphql.config.yaml` file.

must_cover.text: Export the GraphQL schema of every GraphQL service in a file with `bal graphql -i service.bal -o ./schema`, which writes SDL files
Export the schema of one service by its base path with `bal graphql -i service.bal -o ./schema -s /starwars`

Generate a Ballerina GraphQL service from an SDL schema with `bal graphql -i schema.graphql -m service -o ./service`, which writes one file with the service and one with the types, mapping GraphQL object types to service classes by default

Use `-r`/`--use-records-for-objects` to generate record types for GraphQL object types, and know that types with fields that take arguments, types that are members of a union and types that implement an interface are still generated as service classes
Select the operation with `-m schema|service|client`, or let the tool infer it from the input file (a `.bal` service, a `.graphql` schema or a GraphQL config file)

Prepare client generation by writing named queries and mutations in `.graphql` documents and a `graphql.config.yaml` with `schema` (a file path or the endpoint URL) and `documents` (paths to the documents); each operation name becomes a remote method name

Generate a client with `bal graphql -i graphql.config.yaml [-o <dir>]` (experimental), which validates the queries against the schema and writes `client.bal`, `utils.bal`, `types.bal` and `config_types.bal`

Call a GraphQL API through the generated client, e.g. `GraphqlClient countryClient = check new ("https://countries.trevorblades.com/");` then `CountryByCodeResponse response = check countryClient->countryByCode("LK");`
Generate a client for a secured GraphQL API by giving the schema as the endpoint URL and adding headers under `extensions: endpoints: default: headers:` in `graphql.config.yaml`
List several documents under `documents` to generate one client that has a remote method for every query and mutation across them
Generate one Ballerina module per API by declaring `projects:` (each with its own `schema` and `documents`) in `graphql.config.yaml`

out_of_scope: Writing GraphQL services and clients by hand (lib.graphql)
nodes.notes: Client generation is marked experimental in the docs. The docs also list `bal tool update graphql` for updating the tool.

nodes.title: bal grpc
nodes.summary: The `bal grpc` CLI tool compiles a Protocol Buffers (`.proto`) service definition into a Ballerina stub file and, optionally, a service or client template that uses the `ballerina/grpc` module.

must_cover.text: Write the `.proto` input for the tool: `syntax = "proto3";`, an optional `package`, a `service` with `rpc` methods and the `message` types they use

Generate only the stub with `bal grpc --input helloworld.proto --output stubs`, which writes `helloworld_pb.bal` holding the message record types, the client classes and the descriptor constant, and copy it into the Ballerina package that uses it

Generate the stub plus a service template with `bal grpc --input helloworld.proto --mode service --output <dir>`, which writes `helloworld_pb.bal` and `greeter_service.bal`; with several services in one definition you get a shared stub and one template per service

Implement a service from the template: `@grpc:Descriptor {value: HELLOWORLD_DESC}` on `service "Greeter" on grpcListener` (the descriptor maps the service to the definition and must not be changed) with `remote function sayHello(HelloRequest value) returns HelloReply|error`

Generate the stub plus a client template with `bal grpc --input helloworld.proto --mode client --output <dir>`, which writes `helloworld_pb.bal` and `greeter_client.bal` (a `main` function with a client declaration)
Call a service through the generated client class: `GreeterClient ep = check new ("http://localhost:9090");` then `HelloReply reply = check ep->sayHello({name: "Ballerina"});`

Use `google.protobuf` wrapper types such as `google.protobuf.StringValue` in a definition and get plain Ballerina types in the generated code (`remote function hello(string request) returns string`, `string result = check ep->hello("WSO2");`)

Use the stub types generated for streaming RPCs: a client call returning `stream<string, grpc:Error?>` for server streaming, a `<Rpc>StreamingClient` (e.g. `LotsOfGreetingsStreamingClient`) with `send<Type>`, `complete` and `receive<Type>` for client and bidirectional streaming, and a `<Service><Type>Caller` (e.g. `ChatStringCaller`) parameter in the service method

Use the generated `Context<Type>` records (e.g. `ContextString` with `content` and `headers` fields) and their `<rpc>Context` client methods to send and read headers, reading values with `grpc:getHeader`

Resolve `import` directives in a definition with `--proto-path <dir>` (defaults to the current directory; the input file must be inside it), and pass a directory as `--input` to compile several `.proto` files
Know where output goes without `--output`: a directory named after the definition's `package`, or `temp` in the current location when there is no package

out_of_scope: Writing gRPC services and clients, streaming, security and deadlines (lib.grpc)
nodes.notes: The docs list `bal tool update grpc`. They state that Protocol Buffers serialization is only supported in the gRPC module, so the tool only generates code for gRPC service definitions. No `ballerina/protobuf` import in generated stubs was confirmed, so there is no lib.protobuf edge.

nodes.title: bal openapi
nodes.summary: The `bal openapi` CLI tool generates Ballerina HTTP service skeletons, service contract types and clients from an OpenAPI 3.x contract, exports OpenAPI contracts from Ballerina services, and works with the `@openapi` annotations that add metadata, examples and compile-time contract validation.

must_cover.text: Generate an HTTP service skeleton from a contract with `bal openapi -i <contract> --mode service`, which writes `<name>_service.bal` (an `http:Listener` and one `resource function` per operation) plus `types.bal` for the schemas, then fill in the resource bodies

Generate a service contract type with `bal openapi -i <contract> --mode service --with-service-contract`, which writes `service_contract.bal` declaring a `service object { *http:ServiceContract; ... }` type annotated with `@http:ServiceConfig {basePath: ...}`, and implement services against it

Generate a client from a contract with `bal openapi -i <contract> --mode client`, which writes `client.bal` (an `isolated client class Client`), `types.bal` and `utils.bal`, and call the API through the generated client; omitting `--mode` generates both service and client
Choose the generated client method style with `--client-methods resource|remote` (resource methods by default) and call the generated client with resource-access or remote-method call syntax to match
Generate code for only part of a contract with `--tags "tag1","tag2"` or `--operations "op1","op2"`
Use `-n`/`--nullable` to generate nilable field types when a contract's schema properties may come back as `null` without being marked `nullable: true`, avoiding data-binding errors
Generate a boilerplate `test.bal` covering every method of the generated client with `bal openapi -i <contract> --mode client --with-tests`
Generate client methods that bind responses by status code with `--status-code-binding`
Control generated output with `-o <dir>` (output location), `--single-file` (client or service with its types and utilities in one file) and `--license <file>` (license header on generated files)
Generate a mock client that returns the examples documented in the contract with `bal openapi -i <contract> --mode client --mock`, for testing integrations before swapping in the real client

Export an OpenAPI contract from a Ballerina HTTP service (or service contract type) with `bal openapi -i service.bal`, selecting one service by base path with `-s "/hello"`, JSON output with `--json` (YAML by default) and a location with `-o`

Set the info section of an exported contract with `@openapi:ServiceInfo {title: ..., version: ..., description: ..., email: ..., contactName: ..., contactURL: ..., termsOfService: ..., licenseName: ..., licenseURL: ...}` on a service; without it the title defaults to the base path and the version to the package version
Set per-operation metadata with `@openapi:ResourceInfo {operationId: ..., summary: ..., tags: [...]}` on a resource function

Add response and request-body examples to an exported contract through the `examples` field of `@openapi:ResourceInfo`, keyed by `"response"` (status code, media type, example name) or `"requestBody"` (media type, example name), each given as an inline `value` or a `filePath` to a JSON file
Attach a single example to a record type, record field or parameter with `@openapi:Example {value: ...}`, or several named examples with `@openapi:Examples {Name: {value: ...}}`

Validate a service against a contract at compile time with `@openapi:ServiceInfo {contract: "openapi.yaml"}`, narrowing the check with `tags`, `operations`, `excludeTags` or `excludeOperations` and turning it off with `failOnErrors: false`
Set `embed: true` in `@openapi:ServiceInfo` to embed the generated OpenAPI document in the service for introspection endpoint support

Generate a client during `bal build` instead of committing generated code by adding a `[[tool.openapi]]` table to `Ballerina.toml` with mandatory `id` and `filePath`, an optional `targetModule`, and `options.mode`, `options.tags`, `options.operations`, `options.nullable`, `options.license`, `options.clientMethods` or `options.statusCodeBinding`, or add the table with `bal openapi add -i <contract> --id <id> --module <module> [--package <path>]`

Rewrite a contract to Ballerina naming conventions with `bal openapi align -i <contract>`, which adds `x-ballerina-name` extensions and renames schemas (options `-o`, `-n` default `aligned_ballerina_openapi`, `-f json|yaml`, `-t`, `--operations`)

Move inline schemas into `components` with `bal openapi flatten -i <contract>` (for example an inline response object becomes `InlineResponse200`), with the same `-o`, `-n` (default `flattened_openapi`), `-f`, `-t` and `--operations` options

out_of_scope: Writing HTTP services and clients by hand (lib.http)
General `[[tool.*]]` table syntax and other Ballerina.toml settings (tool.ballerina_toml)
Designing REST APIs (topic.rest_api)
nodes.notes: The docs list `bal tool update openapi` for updating the tool. `--use-sanitized-oas` is documented as experimental and left out. The Ballerina.toml tool config documents only client mode.

nodes.title: bal persist
nodes.summary: The `bal persist` CLI tool sets up bal persist in a package and generates the type-safe client, derived types, configurables and SQL scripts from a data model in the `persist` directory, either at every `bal build` or once with `bal persist generate`; it can also build the model from an existing database and generate migration scripts.

must_cover.text: Define the data model in one `.bal` file in the `persist` directory (default `model.bal`) with `import ballerina/persist as _;` and at least one entity record type whose `readonly` field(s) form the primary key

Set up build-integrated generation with `bal persist add --datastore mysql --module store --test-datastore h2`, which creates `persist/model.bal` and adds a `[[tool.persist]]` table (`id`, `targetModule`, `options.datastore`, `options.testDatastore`, `filePath`) to `Ballerina.toml`; it runs only once per project
Choose `--datastore` from `inmemory` (the `add` default), `mysql`, `mssql`, `postgresql`, `h2`, `googlesheets` and `redis`, and `--test-datastore` as `inmemory` (non-SQL) or `h2` (SQL)

Run `bal build` after `bal persist add` to generate `persist_client.bal`, `persist_types.bal`, `persist_db_config.bal`, `script.sql` and, with a test datastore, `persist_test_client.bal` and (for `h2`) `persist_test_init.bal` under `generated/<module>/`, and to create or update `Config.toml`
Supply the configurables generated in `persist_db_config.bal` (for MySQL `host`, `port`, `user`, `password`, `database`) through `Config.toml`, and run the generated `script.sql` to create the tables
Set up one-time generation with `bal persist init`, which only creates the `persist` directory and a `model.bal` with `import ballerina/persist as _;`

Generate the client once with `bal persist generate --datastore mysql --module store --test-datastore h2` (`--datastore` is required), which writes the files into `modules/store/` (or the root module without `--module`)

Create `persist/model.bal` from an existing MySQL, MSSQL or PostgreSQL database with `bal persist pull --datastore mysql --host localhost --port 3306 --user root --database db` (the password is prompted for; unsupported column types are commented out with `[Unsupported[DATA_TYPE]]`), then run `bal persist generate`

Generate migration scripts for model changes with `bal persist migrate <label>` (experimental, MySQL only), which creates `persist/migrations/<timestamp>_<label>/` with `model.bal` and `script.sql`; the datastore cannot be changed once migrations exist

Use the generated client, which is always named `Client`: `Client sClient = check new ();` reads its connection from `Config.toml`, and the derived types such as `EmployeeInsert` and `EmployeeUpdate` go to its resource methods (e.g. `sClient->/employees.post([employee])`)

Tune the generated SQL client's connection pool in `Config.toml` under `[ballerina.sql]` (`maxOpenConnections`, `maxConnectionLifeTime`, `minIdleConnections`) rather than editing `persist_client.bal`, which is overwritten when the code is regenerated

out_of_scope: Entity relations, data model annotations and the full CRUD/query client API (lib.persist)
Ballerina.toml and Config.toml syntax in general (tool.ballerina_toml, tool.config_toml)
nodes.notes: The docs list `bal tool update persist`. Running `bal persist generate` twice fails if the client's native dependency in Ballerina.toml differs from the current version; remove it and regenerate.

nodes.title: bal scan
nodes.summary: `bal scan` is an experimental static code analysis tool, installed with `bal tool pull scan`. It reports code smells, bugs and vulnerabilities in a package, workspace or file using core and library rules, can produce JSON, SARIF and HTML reports, and can send results to SonarQube.

must_cover.text: Install the scan tool with `bal tool pull scan` and check it with `bal tool list`

Analyze the current package with `bal scan`, a given package with `bal scan mypackage`, a standalone file with `bal scan myfile.bal` or a workspace in dependency order, with results printed and saved as JSON under `target/scan`
Generate an HTML report with `bal scan --scan-report` (written to `target/report`), choose the report format with `--format=sarif` (default `json`) and the output directory with `--target-dir=<path>`

List the rules that apply to a project with `bal scan --list-rules`, reading rule IDs such as `ballerina:1` or `ballerina/io:2`, rule kinds (`CODE_SMELL`, `BUG`, `VULNERABILITY`) and severities (`BLOCKER`, `HIGH`, `MEDIUM`, `LOW`, `INFO`)
Limit analysis with `--include-rules="ballerina:1, ballerina/io:2"` or skip rules with `--exclude-rules="ballerina:1"`

Configure the scan in `Scan.toml` at the package root (or via `[scan]` `configPath` in `Ballerina.toml`) with `[rule]` `include`/`exclude` lists and `[[platform]]` entries, knowing a rule set cannot both include and exclude rules

Report results to SonarQube with a `[[platform]]` entry (`name = "sonarqube"`, `path` to the platform plugin JAR, `sonarProjectPropertiesPath`), the `SONAR_TOKEN` environment variable and `bal scan` or `bal scan --platforms="sonarqube"`
Fix rule `ballerina:1` (Avoid checkpanic) by replacing `checkpanic` with `check` and returning the error to the caller instead of panicking
Fix rules `ballerina:2` (unused function parameter) and `ballerina:11` (unused class private fields) by removing or using the unused parameter or private field
Fix rules `ballerina:3` to `ballerina:6` by marking public functions, public methods, public classes and public object types as `isolated`
Fix rules `ballerina:7` to `ballerina:10`: conditions that always evaluate to `true`, `false` or the same value, and variables assigned to themselves
Fix rule `ballerina:12` (invalid range expression) by making the range go in the intended direction, e.g. `foreach int i in 0...9` instead of `9...0`

Fix rules `ballerina:13` (hard-coded secrets) and `ballerina:14` (non-configurable secrets) by reading passwords, API keys, tokens and credential URLs from `configurable string password = ?;` instead of literals or ordinary variables

Fix HTTP rules `ballerina/http:1` by using an explicit accessor such as `resource function delete` instead of `resource function default` for state-changing resources, and `ballerina/http:2` by replacing `allowOrigins: ["*"]` in `@http:ResourceConfig` CORS settings with trusted origins
Fix rules `ballerina/io:2` and `ballerina/log:1` by not printing or logging configurable variables that hold secrets, and `ballerina/log:2` by not writing log files to world-writable directories

Fix crypto rules: `ballerina/crypto:1` by using `crypto:encryptAesGcm` instead of `crypto:encryptAesEcb`/`crypto:encryptAesCbc` and `crypto:encryptRsaEcb` with an OAEP padding such as `crypto:OAEPwithMD5andMGF1` instead of the default `crypto:PKCS1`, `ballerina/crypto:2` by giving `crypto:hashBcrypt` a high work factor (e.g. 14, not 4) and `crypto:hashArgon2` enough memory and iterations, and `ballerina/crypto:3` by not hard-coding initialization vectors

Fix JWT rules `ballerina/jwt:1` to `ballerina/jwt:7`: no weak or `jwt:NONE` algorithms, always set `signatureConfig`, check `issuer` and `audience` in `jwt:validate`, keep `expTime` and `clockSkew` small, keep TLS validation on the JWKS client, and do not trust `jwt:decode` without validation

Fix injection rules `ballerina/os:1` to `ballerina/os:4`, `ballerina/file:1`, `ballerina/file:2` and `ballerina/io:1` by passing `os:exec` arguments as separate list items rather than through `/bin/sh -c`, using absolute executable paths instead of PATH lookup, sanitizing user input used in command arguments and environment variables, validating user-supplied file paths, and not using publicly writable directories for file operations

out_of_scope: Installing and managing tools in general (tool.bal_tool)
Compiler-enforced guarantees that make some rules unnecessary (concept.isolation, concept.errors)
Secure API usage of each library beyond the scan rules (lib.crypto, lib.jwt, lib.http)
nodes.notes: Rule IDs and the rule list follow the current scan-rules page, which also lists `ballerina/http:3`, `ballerina/http:4` (SSRF and open redirect) and `ballerina/email:1` to `ballerina/email:4` (TLS) not itemized here. The doc says `sonarqube` is currently the only platform plugin. The crypto_rules and jwt_rules items summarise several rules each; exact parameter names should be checked against the scan-rules page when generating samples.

nodes.title: bal test
nodes.summary: `bal test` compiles a package (or a single file or a workspace) and runs its test functions. Options select tests and groups, rerun failures, produce HTML, JSON and coverage reports, and run tests in parallel. Test-only configuration comes from `tests/Config.toml` or `-C` arguments.

must_cover.text: Run every test of the current package with `bal test`, which runs the `@test:Config` functions in each module's `tests/` directory and prints passing, failing and skipped counts per module
Test a standalone file with `bal test main_test.bal`, knowing individual `.bal` files that belong to a package cannot be tested on their own
Run selected test functions with `--tests testA,testB`, only from the default module with `--tests PackageName:testName*`, or all tests of a module with `--tests PackageName.ModuleName:*`
Run tests by group: list them with `--list-groups`, include them with `--groups g1,g2` and exclude them with `--disable-groups g2`, for tests tagged with `@test:Config {groups: ["g1"]}`

Run chosen cases of a data-driven test by appending `#` and the case key, e.g. `bal test --tests fruitsDataProviderTest#"banana"` for a map data set or `--tests stringDataProviderTest#1` for an array data set, with `*` wildcards
Rerun only the tests that failed in the previous run with `bal test --rerun-failed`
Generate an HTML test report (plus JSON results) with `bal test --test-report`, showing passed, failed and skipped tests per package and module, and write it elsewhere with `--test-report-dir=<dir>`
Measure line coverage with `bal test --test-report --code-coverage`, which reports package, module and file coverage of source files (test files are excluded)
Produce a JaCoCo XML coverage report for CI tools with `--code-coverage --coverage-format=xml`, and fail the run when coverage is too low with `--min-coverage=80`
Leave files or directories out of coverage with `--excludes`, using paths and globs such as `./generated`, `./modules/**`, `./modules/*/util.bal` or `./*.bal`

Run tests concurrently with `bal test --parallel`, making tests eligible by keeping test, data-provider and setup/teardown functions `isolated` and data-provider parameter types `readonly`, and keep a test sequential with `@test:Config {serialExecution: true}`
Give tests their own configuration in `tests/Config.toml` (e.g. `hostName = "http://localhost:9091/foo"` and `port = 9091`) or with `bal test -Cval1=add -Cval2=10`
Declare Java libraries needed only by tests with `scope = "testOnly"` on a `[[platform.<platform>.dependency]]` entry so they are not packed into the executable
Control testing during builds from `Ballerina.toml` `[build-options]` with `skipTests = true`, `testReport = true` and `codeCoverage = true`
Debug tests remotely by starting them with `bal test --debug <port>` and attaching a debugger
Run tests as a GraalVM native image with `bal test --graalvm` (experimental), passing extra native-image options with `--graalvm-build-options`
Run tests inside a Docker container with `bal test --cloud=docker`, copying test resources in with `[[container.copy.files]]` entries in `Cloud.toml`

out_of_scope: Writing tests with `@test:Config`, assertions, setup/teardown annotations, data providers and mocking (lib.test)
Where tests and test resources live in a package (tool.packages)
Production configuration with Config.toml (tool.config_toml)
nodes.notes: The execute-tests page says `--code-coverage` alone only writes JSON results; the coverage section of the HTML report needs `--test-report --code-coverage`. Parallel and GraalVM test execution are marked experimental.

nodes.title: bal tool
nodes.summary: `bal tool` installs and manages extra CLI tools from Ballerina Central (such as `scan`, `edi`, `health` and `consolidate-packages`), which then run as `bal <tool-id>` subcommands. Tools can also be wired into package builds through `[[tool.<command>]]` entries in `Ballerina.toml`.

must_cover.text: Install a tool with `bal tool pull <tool-id>[:<version>]` (e.g. `bal tool pull scan` or `bal tool pull scan:1.0.0`), which picks the latest version compatible with the current distribution, or from the local repository with `--repository=local`
List installed tools and their active versions with `bal tool list`, and include inactive versions (active ones marked `*`) with `bal tool list --all`
Switch the active version of an installed tool with `bal tool use <tool-id>:<version>` (e.g. `bal tool use health:1.0.0`), adding `--repository=local` for a locally published tool
Update a tool to the latest version compatible with the current distribution and make it active with `bal tool update <tool-id>`
Uninstall one version of a tool with `bal tool remove <tool-id>:<version>` (the active version cannot be removed this way) or every version with `bal tool remove <tool-id>`
Find tools on Ballerina Central with `bal tool search <keyword>`, e.g. `bal tool search health`
Run an installed tool as a `bal` subcommand, e.g. `bal scan` or `bal edi`, and see installed tools under `Tool Commands` in `bal help`

Run a tool as part of `bal build` with a `[[tool.<command>]]` entry (or `[[tool.<command>.<subcommand>]]`) giving a unique `id` (alphanumerics and single underscores, not at the start or end), the spec `filePath`, a unique `targetModule` and `options.<name>` values

Use the `consolidate-packages` tool to build several services into one executable, through `[[tool.consolidate-packages]]` with `options.services = ["myorg/order", "myorg/checkout"]` or the CLI `bal consolidate-packages new --package-path <path> <services>`, `add` and `remove`

out_of_scope: What individual tools do (tool.bal_scan, tool.bal_edi, tool.bal_openapi, ...)
How tool versions are recorded in Dependencies.toml (tool.dependencies_toml)
Managing Ballerina distributions with `bal dist` (tool.bal)
nodes.notes: The help text for `bal tool` lists pull/remove/update/list/search; `bal tool use` has its own help file and is listed on the CLI commands page. How to author and publish a new bal tool (BalTool.toml) is not described in the learn docs I found, so it is left out.

nodes.title: bal wsdl
nodes.summary: The `bal wsdl` CLI tool (pulled from Ballerina Central) generates Ballerina SOAP client classes and XML-bound record types from a WSDL file, for calling SOAP web services through `ballerina/soap`.

must_cover.text: Install the tool from Ballerina Central with `bal tool pull wsdl` before using the `bal wsdl` command

Generate clients and record types for all operations with `bal wsdl calculator.wsdl` run inside a Ballerina package, which writes `client.bal` (possibly several client files) and `types.bal` into the default module
Put the generated client and types in a submodule with `bal wsdl <wsdl-file> --module custom` (`-m`), producing `modules/custom/client.bal` and `modules/custom/types.bal`
Generate client methods only for selected operations with `--operations http://sample.org/action1,http://sample.org/action2` (a comma-separated list of operation URIs)
Generate a client only for one WSDL port with `--port <port-name>` (`-p`); without it a client is generated for every port

Call a SOAP service through a generated client such as `CalculatorSoap12Client`: an `isolated client class` wrapping a `soap12:Client` whose `init` takes `string serviceUrl` (defaulting to the WSDL address) and `*soap:ClientConfig`, with one remote method per operation that takes the request envelope record and returns the response envelope record

sources.note: expected generated client in the tool's tests

must_cover.text: Build request values from the generated envelope records (`...SoapRequest` with optional `Header` and a `Body` holding the operation element), which carry `@xmldata:Name {value: "Envelope"}` and `@xmldata:Namespace` annotations so they convert to SOAP XML with `xmldata:toXml` and back with `xmldata:parseAsType`

sources.note: expected generated types in the tool's tests

out_of_scope: Writing SOAP clients by hand and SOAP security (lib.soap)
XML data binding in general (lib.data.xmldata)
nodes.notes: The learn page documents only the command and its options. The shape of the generated client and types comes from the expected output in the wsdl-tools test resources (calculator.bal), which may differ between tool versions.

nodes.title: Ballerina.toml
nodes.summary: The `Ballerina.toml` manifest identifies a package and holds its metadata, build options, dependency overrides, Java platform libraries and build-time tool entries.

must_cover.text: Write the `[package]` table with `org`, `name` and `version`, knowing `bal new` defaults `org` to the machine user name, the directory name is used when `name` is missing, and generated manifests also record `distribution = "2201.x.y"`
Add Ballerina Central metadata to `[package]` with `readme = "docs/Reference.md"`, `icon = "icon.png"` (PNG only), `keywords`, `authors`, `repository` and `license = ["Apache-2.0"]`

Make a package private with `visibility = "private"` in `[package]`, so only members of its organization can see and use it, which requires an access token in `Settings.toml` to consume it as a dependency
Pack extra files into the BALA with `include = ["documents", "sample.png"]`, using path patterns such as `*.html`, `/bar`, `baz/`, `**/grault/garply`, `waldo/xyzzy/**` and exclusions like `!corge.rs`

Describe non-default modules with `[[package.modules]]` entries giving `name = "winery.foo"`, `export = true` to make the module public (only the default module is public by default) and a module-specific `readme`

Set build options in `[build-options]` instead of passing CLI flags: `observabilityIncluded`, `offline`, `skipTests`, `testReport`, `codeCoverage`, `cloud = "k8s"`, `graalvm` and `graalvmBuildOptions`

Declare a `[[dependency]]` entry with `org`, `name` and `version` to set the minimum version of a dependency, so the latest compatible version at or above it is resolved (e.g. to move `ballerinax/mysql` to a newer minor version)

Resolve a dependency from the local repository by adding `repository = "local"` to its `[[dependency]]` entry, knowing a newer patch version in the distribution or Central repositories still takes priority

Bundle Java libraries with `[[platform.java21.dependency]]` entries giving Maven `groupId`, `artifactId` and `version` (resolved into `target/platform-libs`), and add private Maven repositories with `[[platform.<platform>.repository]]` (`id`, `url`, `username`, `password`)

Bundle a local JAR with `path = "<path-to-jar>"`, restrict it to some modules with `modules = [...]`, and give `groupId`, `artifactId` and `version` so that conflicting versions of the same JAR resolve to the latest one

Set `scope = "testOnly"` on a platform dependency used only by tests, or `scope = "provided"` to keep it out of the BALA (then `groupId`, `artifactId` and `version` are mandatory and consumers must declare it themselves)
Mark Java dependencies as GraalVM compatible with `graalvmCompatible = true` on each `[[platform.java21.dependency]]` or for the whole package with `[platform.java21]` `graalvmCompatible = true`

Run code generation tools before the build with `[[tool.<command>]]` entries giving `id`, `filePath`, `targetModule` and `options.*`, for example `[[tool.openapi]]` with `id = "client01"`, `filePath = "./openapi.yaml"` and `options.mode = "client"`
Point the formatter and the scan tool at their configuration files with `[format]` `configPath = "Format.toml"` and `[scan]` `configPath = "path/to/Scan.toml"` (a local path or an HTTP/HTTPS URL)

out_of_scope: Package and module layout (tool.packages)
The auto-generated Dependencies.toml and version resolution rules (tool.dependencies_toml)
Runtime values in Config.toml (tool.config_toml)
Cloud.toml and Kubernetes/Docker artifact options (tool.code_to_cloud)
GraalVM native image builds (tool.graalvm)
Calling Java code from Ballerina (concept.external_functions, lib.jballerina.java)

sources.note: Real manifest using platform.java21 and distribution

nodes.notes: The learn docs still show `[[platform.java11.dependency]]`; current distributions (2201.13, see the ballerina/log manifest) use `java21`. Items use `java21`; reviewers may want to mention both. `distribution` is not described on the package-references page but appears in generated manifests and in the customize-formatting example.

nodes.title: Ballerina Central
nodes.summary: Ballerina Central is the public package repository. Packages are packed into BALA archives with `bal pack`, published with `bal push`, found with `bal search`, fetched with `bal pull` and deprecated with `bal deprecate`. Custom Maven repositories can host private packages or proxy Central.

must_cover.text: Create the distribution archive with `bal pack`, which writes `target/bala/<org>-<name>-any-<version>.bala`, after adding the `README.md` that publishing requires

Authenticate to Central by putting an access token from the Central dashboard in `<USER_HOME>/.ballerina/Settings.toml` under `[central]` `accesstoken="<token>"`, or in the `BALLERINA_CENTRAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` environment variable for CI, knowing tokens expire after one year
Set `org` in `Ballerina.toml` to a Central organization you belong to before pushing, knowing names starting with `ballerina` (`ballerina`, `ballerinax`, ...) are reserved
Publish with `bal push` (or `bal push <bala-path>`), knowing a published version is permanent and cannot be overwritten or removed, so new changes need a new version
Check a package before publishing by pushing it to the local repository with `bal push --repository local` and depending on it from another package

Check whether local API changes fit the next version number with `bal semver`, comparing against a given release with `-c <version>`/`--compare-version` and showing the source diff with `-d`/`--show-diff`
Download a package and its dependencies into the user cache with `bal pull <org>/<package>[:<version>]`, e.g. `bal pull wso2/gmail:1.1.0`, or from a custom repository with `--repository=<id>`
Find packages with `bal search <keyword>`, which matches organization and package names case-insensitively, and help users find your package with `keywords` in `Ballerina.toml`

Deprecate all versions or one version of a published package with `bal deprecate <org>/<package>[:<version>] --message="..."`, and reverse it with `--undo`, knowing deprecated versions are hidden from search and builds warn when they are used
Publish a private package with `visibility = "private"` so it is visible only to members of the organization who are logged in, and set up `Settings.toml` with a token to pull it

Configure custom Maven repositories (Nexus, Artifactory, GitHub or GitLab packages) in `Settings.toml` with `[[repository.maven]]` entries (`id`, `url`, `username`, `accesstoken`), then `bal push --repository <id>` and `bal pull ... --repository=<id>`
Send all Central traffic through a Maven proxy repository with a single `[[repository.maven]]` entry marked `proxyCentral = true` (more than one such entry is an error)

sources.note: Proxy Ballerina Central with a Maven repository

must_cover.text: Reach Central through an HTTP proxy by adding `[proxy]` with `host`, `port`, `username` and `password` to `Settings.toml`

Publish from CI, e.g. a GitHub Actions workflow using `ballerina-platform/setup-ballerina@v1` that runs `bal test`, `bal pack` and `bal push` with `BALLERINA_CENTRAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` taken from a repository secret

out_of_scope: Writing package metadata keys (tool.ballerina_toml)
How builds resolve and lock dependency versions (tool.dependencies_toml)
Pulling CLI tools with `bal tool pull` (tool.bal_tool)
nodes.notes: The docs call `bal semver` an experimental tool (available from Swan Lake Update 2).

nodes.title: Code to Cloud
nodes.summary: Code to Cloud is a compiler extension that generates Dockerfiles, container images and Kubernetes or OpenShift YAML from a Ballerina package at build time (`--cloud=docker|k8s|openshift` or `[build-options] cloud`), with defaults derived from the code and overrides in `Cloud.toml`; the same `cloud` build option also packages AWS Lambda and Azure Functions deployments.

must_cover.text: Turn on artifact generation with `cloud = "docker"` or `cloud = "k8s"` under `[build-options]` in `Ballerina.toml` and run `bal build`, or pass it inline with `bal build --cloud=docker` (also for a single file: `bal build --cloud=k8s hello.bal`)

Build a Docker image from a service package with `--cloud=docker`, which writes a Dockerfile under `target/docker/`, builds the image (one container per package, exposing the listener ports) and prints a `docker run -d -p 9090:9090 <repository>/<name>:<tag>` command
Override image settings in `Cloud.toml` under `[container.image]` (`repository`, `name`, `tag`, `base`, `entrypoint`) and the user under `[container.image.user]` (`run_as`)

Control generation in `Cloud.toml` under `[settings]`: `buildImage = false` to only write the Dockerfile, `singleYAML` for one YAML file with all artifacts, and `thinJar` to use thin JARs in the container
Copy extra files into the image with `[[container.copy.files]]` entries (`sourceFile`, `target`)

Provide `Config.toml` at runtime, since it is not packed into the image: mount it in Docker with `docker run -v <path>/Config.toml:/home/ballerina/Config.toml ...`, or in Kubernetes with `[[cloud.config.files]] file = "./Config.toml"`, which creates a ConfigMap, mounts it and sets `BAL_CONFIG_FILES`

Generate Kubernetes artifacts with `--cloud=k8s`, which builds the Docker image and writes a YAML file under `target/kubernetes/<module>/` with a Service for the exposed ports, a Deployment and a HorizontalPodAutoscaler; push the image (or build against Minikube after `eval $(minikube docker-env)`), then `kubectl apply -f target/kubernetes/<module>` and `kubectl expose deployment <name>-deployment --type=NodePort` for local testing

Set container resources in `Cloud.toml` under `[cloud.deployment]` (`min_memory`, `max_memory`, `min_cpu`, `max_cpu`, which become the Deployment's requests and limits) along with `internal_domain_name` and `external_accessible`
Configure the generated HorizontalPodAutoscaler under `[cloud.deployment.autoscaling]` with `min_replicas`, `max_replicas`, `cpu` and `memory` utilisation thresholds, or `enable = false`

Add liveness and readiness probes with `[cloud.deployment.probes.liveness]` and `[cloud.deployment.probes.readiness]` (`port`, `path`), backed by a separate probe service in the code, e.g. `service /probes on new http:Listener(9091)` with `resource function get healthz()` and `get readyz()`

Supply configuration and secrets to Kubernetes with `[[cloud.config.maps]]` and `[[cloud.secret.files]]` (`file`, `mount_dir`), `[[cloud.config.envs]]` (`key_ref`, `name`, `config_name`), `[[cloud.secret.envs]]` (`key_ref`, `name`, `secret_name`) and `[[cloud.config.secrets]]` (`file`, `name`)
Declare persistent volumes with `[[cloud.deployment.storage.volumes]]` (`name`, `local_path`, `size`)
Run a `main` function as a Kubernetes cron job by annotating it with `@cloud:Task {schedule: {minutes: "*", hours: "*", dayOfMonth: "*", monthOfYear: "*", daysOfWeek: "*"}}` from `ballerina/cloud`
Generate OpenShift artifacts with `cloud = "openshift"` (or `bal build --cloud=openshift`), written to `target/openshift/`, and deploy them with `oc apply -f target/openshift/<module>`

Customise the generated YAML with Kustomize (`resources` pointing at the files in `target/kubernetes/` plus patches) and automate deployment in GitHub Actions with `ballerina-platform/ballerina-action` and `args: build --cloud=k8s`, then `docker push` and `kubectl apply`

Package functions for AWS Lambda by annotating them with `@lambda:Function` from `ballerinax/aws.lambda` (signature `function (lambda:Context, json|EventType) returns json|error`, e.g. `lambda:SQSEvent`, `lambda:S3Event`) and building with `bal build --cloud="aws_lambda"` (a ZIP) or `--cloud="aws_lambda_image"` (a container image), then deploying with the printed AWS CLI command

Build an Azure Functions package with `bal build --cloud="azure_functions"` (or `azure_functions_local` for local runs), and run it with `func start --script-root target/azure_functions` or publish it with `func azure functionapp publish <app> --script-root target/azure_functions`

out_of_scope: Native images with `--graalvm` (tool.graalvm)
Writing the HTTP services being deployed (lib.http)
Writing Azure Functions triggers and bindings in code (not covered by a node)
nodes.notes: macOS on Apple Silicon needs `export DOCKER_DEFAULT_PLATFORM=linux/amd64` before building images (per the docs). The Dockerfile sample in the docs shows `FROM ballerina/jvm-runtime:1.0`, while the spec gives `ballerina/jvm-runtime:2.0` as the default `base`. The spec shows `[[settings]]` but the docs use `[settings]`; items follow the docs.

nodes.title: Config.toml
nodes.summary: Values for `configurable` variables are supplied at runtime through TOML content (a `Config.toml` file, `BAL_CONFIG_FILES` or `BAL_CONFIG_DATA`), `-Ckey=value` command-line arguments or `BAL_CONFIG_VAR_*` environment variables.

must_cover.text: Supply values in a `Config.toml` file in the current working directory, which `bal run` and the built program read by default, e.g. `port = 8080` for `configurable int port = 9090;`
Give a value for every `configurable` declared with `= ?` (the program exits with an error if one is missing), and override defaulted ones such as `configurable int port = 9090;` only when needed

Write TOML values for scalar configurables: `boolean`, `int` and `byte` as integers, `float` and `decimal` as floats, `string` as a string, `xml` as a string such as `book = "<book>The Lost World</book>"`, and an enum by its member value such as `country = "Sri Lanka"`

Write TOML arrays for array and tuple configurables, e.g. `ports = [9090, 9091]`, `acceptTypes = ["application/xml", "application/json"]` and `student = ["Jane", 1101, ["Maths", "English"], {level = 4, class = "B"}, 98]`

Configure record and map values as TOML tables, e.g. `[person]` with `name = "John"` and `age = 45`, nested record fields with dotted keys like `food.name = "carrot"`, or inline tables like `admin = {username = "admin", password = "password"}`

Configure `Person[]`, `map<string>[]` and `table<...>` values (e.g. `configurable UserTable & readonly users = ?;`) as arrays of tables with repeated `[[users]]` headers or an inline array of tables, and `table<...>[]` as a 2-D array of inline tables

Supply union, `anydata` and `json` configurables with the TOML type that matches the value, e.g. `code = "10001A"` for `int|string`, `data = 123` and `payload = {name = "Jane"}`, and give nil-typed configurables a default because TOML has no nil value

Configure variables of non-root modules and of dependency packages with `[org-name.module-name]` tables or dotted keys such as `myapp.port = 9090`, knowing the org and module parts are optional only for the root module of the root package

Configure library behaviour through their configurables in TOML, e.g. `[ballerina.log]` with `level = "ERROR"` and `format = "logfmt"`, or `[ballerina.observe]` with `enabled = true`, `metricsEnabled` and `tracingEnabled`

List one or more TOML files in the `BAL_CONFIG_FILES` environment variable with the OS path separator (`:` on Linux/macOS, `;` on Windows), where earlier files take precedence and `Config.toml` is no longer read unless it is listed too
Pass TOML content directly in the `BAL_CONFIG_DATA` environment variable, e.g. `export BAL_CONFIG_DATA='maxPayload=1.0'`, when no config file can be mounted

Override values on the command line with `-Ckey=value` after `--`, e.g. `bal run -- -Cport=9090 -Cname=John`, using module-qualified keys `[[org.]module.]variable` and the `toString()` form, for `int`, `byte`, `float`, `boolean`, `string`, `decimal`, enum and `xml` only

Set single values with `BAL_CONFIG_VAR_<KEY>` environment variables (e.g. `export BAL_CONFIG_VAR_PORT=9090`), where module-qualified keys become `ORGNAME_MODULENAME_VARIABLE` in upper case with dots replaced by underscores, supported for the same simple types as `-C` (Swan Lake Update 9 and later)
Explain the override order when values come from several places: `BAL_CONFIG_VAR_*` environment variables win over `-C` arguments, which win over TOML content

Keep passwords and tokens in a separate TOML file listed first in `BAL_CONFIG_FILES` (for example a Kubernetes secret mounted as a volume) and read them through `configurable string password = ?;` instead of hard-coding them

out_of_scope: Declaring `configurable` variables and the allowed types in the language (concept.variables)
Test-specific `tests/Config.toml` and `bal test -C` (tool.bal_test)
Cloud.toml and Kubernetes ConfigMap/Secret generation (tool.code_to_cloud)
Settings.toml for Central access tokens and proxies (tool.central)

sources.note: Supplying values to configurable variables (TOML keys, resolution, file lookup)

nodes.notes: The configurable spec says the TOML file lookup also applies to `java -jar`; the learn docs only show `bal run`. Precedence follows the note at the top of the provide-values page.

nodes.title: Dependencies.toml
nodes.summary: The compiler resolves package dependencies automatically from import declarations and records the chosen versions in the CLI-managed `Dependencies.toml`, which, together with SemVer compatibility rules and the sticky and offline modes, controls which versions later builds use.

must_cover.text: Explain automatic dependency resolution: the compiler finds the packages behind `import` declarations and picks the latest compatible versions from the distribution repository, Ballerina Central, configured custom repositories and the local repository, with no dependency list to maintain

Explain that the first `bal build` generates `Dependencies.toml` at the package root, that the CLI manages it (it should not be edited by hand), and that versions locked there are treated as minimum versions in later builds

Read a generated `Dependencies.toml`: the `[ballerina]` table with `dependencies-toml-version` and `distribution-version`, and `[[package]]` entries with `org`, `name`, `version`, `dependencies`, `modules` and `scope = "testOnly"` for test-only packages
Explain that builds pick up new patch versions of dependencies automatically, that this check runs at most once a day, and that running `bal clean` makes the next build check again
Move a dependency to a newer minor version by declaring that version as a minimum in a `Ballerina.toml` `[[dependency]]` entry, e.g. `org = "ballerinax"`, `name = "mysql"`, `version = "1.5.0"`

Build with the exact versions locked in `Dependencies.toml` using `bal build --sticky`, which turns off automatic updates (also available on `bal run`, `bal test`, `bal pack`, `bal doc` and `bal graph`)

Build without network access using `--offline` (or `offline = true` in `[build-options]`), resolving only from the distribution repository and local caches, and combine `--offline --sticky` for predictable, fast builds

Apply the compatibility rule that two versions are compatible only if their major versions are equal and non-zero, so `0.2.3` and `0.2.4` are incompatible, `1.2.3` and `1.4.5` are compatible, and `1.2.3-beta` is newer than `1.2.3-alpha.2`

Explain that when the dependency graph contains several versions of a package the latest compatible one wins, and incompatible versions fail the build with `Two incompatible versions exist in the dependency graph`
Explain that switching a package to a new Swan Lake update distribution makes the compiler update `Dependencies.toml` to the latest compatible minor versions for that distribution
Inspect the resolved dependency graph with `bal graph` (DOT output) for a package or a single `.bal` file, and print intermediate resolution graphs with `bal graph --dump-raw-graphs`

Explain that a deprecated package version is used only when it is already locked and the build is `--sticky`, or when no other compatible version exists, and that the build then warns with the deprecation message

Explain that build tools declared with `[[tool.<command>]]` are resolved like packages from the distribution and Central repositories, and their versions are recorded in `Dependencies.toml` as minimum versions
Clear cached dependencies of the current package or workspace with `bal clean --dependency-cache`, and print dependency diagnostics hidden by default with `--show-dependency-diagnostics`

out_of_scope: Writing `[[dependency]]` and platform entries in Ballerina.toml (tool.ballerina_toml)
Import declarations in the language (concept.modules_imports)
Publishing and deprecating packages, custom Maven repositories (tool.central)
nodes.notes: The ballerina-spec package spec still describes an older `[[dependency]]` format for Dependencies.toml; the file_structure item follows real generated files (dependencies-toml-version 2).

nodes.title: GraalVM
nodes.summary: Since Swan Lake Update 7 (2201.7.0), `bal build --graalvm` compiles a package ahead-of-time into a standalone GraalVM native executable instead of an uber JAR, either with a local GraalVM or inside a Docker build, with options to tune the native-image build, run tests natively and mark Java dependencies as GraalVM-compatible.

must_cover.text: Explain the trade-off between the JIT-run uber JAR from `bal build` and the AOT native executable from `bal build --graalvm`: millisecond startup, a fraction of the resources, no warmup, smaller container images and a reduced attack surface, against a long, memory- and CPU-heavy build

Set up a local native build: install GraalVM (e.g. `sdk install java 21.0.2-graalce`), set `GRAALVM_HOME`, and match the JDK to the Ballerina update (Java 11 up to Update 7, 17 for Updates 8 to 10, 21 from Update 11); on Windows use Microsoft Visual C++ and the x64 Native Tools Command Prompt

Build a native executable with `bal build --graalvm`, which writes `target/bin/<package>` containing the package's modules, its dependencies, the Ballerina runtime and statically linked JDK native code, and run it directly (`./target/bin/hello_world`)

Build the native executable inside Docker without a local GraalVM using `bal build --graalvm --cloud=docker`, which generates a multi-stage Dockerfile (a `ghcr.io/graalvm/native-image-community` build stage running `native-image` and a `gcr.io/distroless/base` runtime stage); give Docker at least 8GB of memory

Pass native-image options with `graalvmBuildOptions = "..."` (and `graalvm = true`) under `[build-options]` in `Ballerina.toml`, or with `bal build --graalvm --graalvm-build-options="-H:+StaticExecutableWithDynamicLibC"`
Run tests against a native image with `bal test --graalvm` (it also accepts `--graalvm-build-options`), knowing that code coverage and runtime debugging are not supported in native test runs

Act on the build warning that lists dependencies pending GraalVM verification or marked incompatible: test the native image with `bal test --graalvm` (for example as a daily CI job) and, if needed, replace the packages; packages that only use the Ballerina library or Java libraries shipped with the distribution are inferred to be compatible

Mark a library package that uses Java platform libraries as GraalVM-compatible after verifying it with `bal test --graalvm`, by setting `graalvmCompatible = true` under `[platform.java21]` (or on each `[[platform.java21.dependency]]` entry) in `Ballerina.toml`, which removes the `bal pack` warning

Combine `--graalvm` with serverless targets, e.g. `bal build --cloud="aws_lambda" --graalvm` for a smaller, faster-starting Lambda function, or `bal build --cloud="azure_functions_local" --graalvm` and `--cloud="azure_functions" --graalvm` for Azure Functions

out_of_scope: Docker and Kubernetes artifact generation in general (tool.code_to_cloud)
Java interop bindings (lib.jballerina.java)

sources.note: Build the GraalVM executable in a container
Ballerina.toml build options and platform compatibility

nodes.notes: The learn docs do not cover reflection configuration or `@java` interop limitations for native images, so they are left out. The docs say GraalVM native-image support on Apple M1 is still experimental.

nodes.title: Packages
nodes.summary: Ballerina code is organized into packages: versioned, shareable units identified by organization, name and version that hold a default module, optional non-default modules, tests and resources. Workspaces group several related packages in one directory tree.

must_cover.text: Create a package with `bal new <package-path>` (or `bal new .` for the current directory), and explain that a directory containing `Ballerina.toml` is a package root and the generated `main.bal` belongs to the default module

Create packages from the built-in templates with `bal new -t main`, `bal new -t service` (a service plus `tests/service_test.bal`) and `bal new -t lib` (a library source file, `README.md` and `tests/lib_test.bal`)

sources.note: Create a service package / library package

must_cover.text: Explain the default module: all `.bal` files at the package root share one namespace, so top-level symbols defined in one file are visible in the others, and the default module is referred to by the package name

Add a non-default module with `bal add <name>`, which creates `modules/<name>/` holding the module `<package-name>.<name>` (e.g. `bal add core.db` in package `app` gives `app.core.db`), where module names contain only alphanumerics, underscores and periods

Import a module of the same package with `import <package>.<module>;` (the org name is optional) and call its `public` symbols through the prefix, e.g. `import hello_world.util;` then `util:properCaseMessage("hello world!")`, optionally renaming with `as`

sources.note: Import a module from the same package

must_cover.text: Import modules of other packages with `import org/module [as prefix];`, including the default module (`import ballerina/io;`) and non-default modules (`import ballerinax/salesforce.bulk as sfBulk;`)

Lay out a package with `Ballerina.toml`, `Dependencies.toml`, `README.md`, root `.bal` files, `tests/`, `resources/`, `modules/`, `generated/` and the build output directory `target/`, knowing which files are generated and which are written by hand

Place each module's unit tests in that module's own `tests/` directory (e.g. `modules/util/tests/`), knowing tests can use the module's non-public symbols while symbols defined in test files are not visible to the module sources

Store package resources such as images and default configs in the root `resources/` directory and test-only files in `tests/resources/`, accessed by absolute path or by a path relative to the package root

Explain the `generated/` directory: `.bal` files at its root merge into the default module, each direct subdirectory merges into the module of the same name, and its `resources` directory holds package resources

Choose valid names: `org` with alphanumerics and underscores, package and module names with alphanumerics, underscores and periods (max 256 characters), and hierarchical package names such as `aws.s3` and `aws.sqs`

Avoid the split module condition (two packages whose latest versions contain the same module) when moving a module such as `aws.rds.mysql` out of package `aws.rds`, by first pushing a new `aws.rds` version without that module

Version packages with SemVer `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`: use `0.x.y` while the API is unstable, pre-release versions such as `1.0.0-alpha` and `1.0.0-alpha.1` while stabilizing, and bump patch, minor or major for bug fixes, compatible additions or breaking changes

Try an unpublished package from another package by running `bal pack` and `bal push --repository local` (stored in `<USER_HOME>/.ballerina/repositories/local/bala`) and adding a `[[dependency]]` entry with `repository = "local"`
Create a workspace with `bal new --workspace <name>`, add packages with `bal new` inside it, and list them in the workspace-level `Ballerina.toml` as `[workspace]` `packages = ["hello-app", "utils"]`
Import a sibling package of a workspace (e.g. `import myorg/utils;`) without publishing it, knowing workspace packages take priority over the distribution and Central repositories during resolution

Build, test and run workspace packages from the workspace root with `bal build`, `bal build <package>`, `bal test` and `bal run <package>`, knowing executables are produced only for packages no other workspace package depends on

out_of_scope: Module and import declaration semantics in the language, such as prefixes and visibility (concept.modules_imports)
Keys of the Ballerina.toml manifest (tool.ballerina_toml)
Dependency version resolution and locking (tool.dependencies_toml)
Publishing to and pulling from Ballerina Central (tool.central)
Writing test functions with the test module (lib.test)

sources.note: Package structure, default and non-default modules
Package layout, module layout, naming and versioning

nodes.notes: The workspaces feature is recent (the docs and `bal new --workspace` help are current as of distribution 2201.13). `bal new` also generates `.gitignore` and `.devcontainer.json` according to its help text.

nodes.title: VS Code extension
nodes.summary: The Ballerina extension for Visual Studio Code adds language support (completion, hover, quick fixes, refactorings), commands that call the `bal` CLI, run and debug support through CodeLens and `launch.json`, visual tools such as the HTTP API Designer and Data Mapper, and Ballerina notebooks.

must_cover.text: Install the Ballerina extension (`WSO2.ballerina`) and activate it by opening a package folder (e.g. `code .`) or several packages as a VS Code multi-root workspace, with the Ballerina version shown in the status bar

Run the Command Palette commands **Ballerina: Build**, **Run**, **Test**, **Pack**, **Build Documentation**, **Add Module** and **Show Examples**, which call `bal build`, `bal run`, `bal test`, `bal pack`, `bal doc` and `bal add`, and **Create 'Cloud.toml'** for code-to-cloud settings
Generate record types from sample JSON with **Paste JSON as Record** (JSON copied to the clipboard) or the Record Editor's **Import A JSON** option with **Make Separate Record Definitions**
Run or debug a `main` function or service with the **Run** and **Debug** CodeLens, and run or debug a single test from the CodeLens shown on its `@test:Config` function

Write `.vscode/launch.json` debug configurations of `"type": "ballerina"`: `Ballerina Debug` (`"request": "launch"` with `programArgs`, `commandOptions`, `env` and `"terminal": "integrated"`), `Ballerina Test` (`"debugTests": true`) and `Ballerina Remote` (`"request": "attach"`)

Debug a program running elsewhere by starting it with `bal run --debug 5005 <package-or-jar>` or `bal test --debug <port>` and attaching a `Ballerina Remote` configuration with `debuggeeHost` and `debuggeePort`

Use Ballerina debugging features: conditional breakpoints with Ballerina expressions, logpoints with `${expr}` string templates, pause and continue, expression evaluation in the Debug Console and Watch window, and the strand and stack trace view

Apply error-handling quick fixes: `Create variable and check error`, `Create variable and type guard`, `Ignore return value` (assign to `_`), `Add 'check' error`, `Surround with do/on-fail` and `Change return type to 'error?'`

Apply type and declaration quick fixes such as `Change variable type`, `Add type cast`, `Create function`, `Implement all`, `Create record`, `Fill record fields`, `Add isolated qualifier`, `Convert to readonly clone` and `Convert module variable to listener declaration`
Fix imports with `Import module`, `Pull unresolved module` (pulls missing packages from Central), `Remove import` and `Remove all unused imports`

Refactor with `Extract to constant`, `Extract to function`, `Extract to local variable` and `Extract type` (anonymous record to a named record type), rewrite array mappings with `Map with a query expression`, and use source actions such as `Create getter and setter`, `Type guard variable` and `Document this`
